Present:
Mr. Pankaj Miglani, Advocate, present for the petitioners in all the writ
petitions.
Mr. K.P. Upadhyay, learned Standing Counsel, present for the State/respondent nos. 1 to 3.

Judgment Dated: 30.10.2013
Honíble Sudhanshu Dhulia, J. (Oral)
 In this bunch of writ petitions, what is under challenge
is an order of Conservator of Forest, Southern Kumaun
Circle, Uttarakhand, Nainital, whereby, according to the
petitioners, the sanction of auction sale, which was granted
in his favour has been cancelled, the power of which,
according to the petitioners does not vest with the
Conservator of Forest, and therefore, inter alia, the order is
totally without jurisdiction.
2. ëResin,í which is derived in forests by tapping pine
trees is a ìforest produceî. It was put for sale by way of
auction by respondent no. 2. The resin, so collected in one
of the units of the forest which is called ìcircleî and which
was under the Conservator of Forest was put for auction on
20th August, 2013. Bids were offered for various lots of
resins.
3. The petitioners, who are before this Court, had,
admittedly raised the highest bid and on the fall of the
hammer in their favour, they would argue, that the sale was
completed in their favour and, subsequently, the forest

3
authorities cannot retract in any way and the same being
done by them now is in violation of law. At the time of the
sale i.e. on 20th August, 2013, the minimum auction price
of the resin was also quoted by the Forest Authorities. The
Divisional Forest Officer, Nainital Forest Division, Nainital
subsequently, sought approval from the Conservator of
Forest, Southern Kumaun Circle, Nainital. The Conservator
of Forest, Southern Kumaun Circle, Nainital after noticing
that for the crop of the Year 2011 and 2012, the average
sale price has been received as `5276.27 and `5566.43 per
quintal.
4. Then learned counsel for the State submitted that on
31st August, 2013 in Champawat Forest Division, the resin
which was collected in the year 2011 has been auctioned
and the price was received to Rs.7505/- per quintal and the
resin which was for the year 2012 has been auctioned at
Rs.7357.09/- per quintal. Learned counsel for the State
further states that on 5th September, 2013 in Almora Forest
Division the resin which was for the year 2012 the average
price was received as Rs.7500/- to Rs.7690/- per quintal.
Hence, noticing the difference of sale price (by way of
auction) of resin at Champawat and Almora, Forest
Divisions on one hand and at Nainital Forest Division on
the other which was more than Rs.2000/- per quintal, the
Conservator of Forest came to the conclusion that the sale
price is low and it is neither in public interest nor in the
interest of the State Exchequer to grant approval to the said
bid and, consequently he refused to give approval. Hence,
aggrieved by the said order of the Conservator of Forest, the
petitioners have challenged the said order by means of the
present writ petitions.

4
5. The main argument of the petitioners before this Court
is that order of the Conservator of Forest is absolutely
without jurisdiction, as the competent authority who can
grant sanction to the auction sale is the Divisional Forest
Officer who has already sanctioned the auction sale. Neither
the conditions of the auction sale under which the sale was
done nor any Rule provide for the Conservator of Forest to
bypass the order of the Divisional Forest Officer and the
same being totally without jurisdiction is liable to be
rejected.
6. The petitioner has placed reliance upon condition no.
5, 6A, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 21 of conditions of auction and these
conditions, if translated in English, are as follows:-
ì5. Upon receiving sanction of the sale of lisa
lots by the competent authority, the same shall be
put on the notice board. Upon being such, the
purchaser of the lots would be deemed to have
received the information of the approval of the lots.
6-A. Purchaser shall have to take the
purchased lisa till 45 days from the date of sanction
of the bid from the office of the Divisional Forest
Officer, upon depositing the entire price (with all
taxes) of the lisa lots.
8. Divisional Forest Officer or Auctioning
Officer shall have full right to accept or reject any
bid without assigning any reason.
9. In the auction, after fall of hammer,
successful bidder, on the basis of the bid 10 % of
the cost of lisa or which the Auctioning Officer
deems fit security will have to deposit. Maximum
amount of the security may be 50 %. After
depositing the security, successful bidder shall
have to sign the papers related to conditions and
related papers. Upon no doing so, action can be
initiated against him under Section 185 of the
Indian Penal Code. Upon completion of the contract,
security can be adjusted or returned towards the
sale price. If purchaser fails to deposit the security

5
money, the auctioning officer shall have full right to
re-auction the lot and forfeit the entry fees.
10. In the auction, after acceptance of the bid
of purchaser, purchaser shall be completely
responsible for the loss or damage of the lisa of the
relevant lot whether it has been caused by any
reason.
21. If there is any contradiction in the
conditions of the sale rule and conditions of lisa
auction notice, conditions of auction notice shall be
binding.î

7. The first reliance of the petitioner is on condition no. 5,
which states that if the notice of sanction is put on the
notice board, it would be deemed to sufficient notice to the
purchaser. His further emphasis is on condition no. 9, 10,
which states that on fall of hammer successful bidder has
to deposit 10% of the total cost of the lisa as security. Once
the bid has accepted with the fall of the hammer the same
cannot be retracted or refused by either party. The learned
counsel for the petitioner says that under condition 10 once
the bid of the petitioner was accepted the entire property in
the goods passed on him and in case there is any harm to
the goods in any manner it would be the sole responsibility
of the purchaser i.e. the present petitioner on whom the
property has been passed on in terms of condition no. 10.
8. Learned Chief Standing Counsel Mr. K.P. Upadhyay,
who represents the State of Uttarakhand in the present
matter, on the other hand, would rely upon condition no.20,
which if translated in English, reads as under:-
ì20.Upon the sale of these lots, prevalent rules
for sale in Northern Kumaun Circle, would also
be applicable.î

6
9. He then argue that the Rules which are presently
enforced in the Northern Kumaun Circle would also be
applicable in the present matter. Condition 3 (a) and 3 (b)
are relevant in this matter, which if translated in English
read as under:-
ì3 (a). The Divisional Forest Officer has got full
power for auction and auction of lots made by
him will consider to be final, provided they have
received the sanction of competent authority.
(b). The bid, accepted at the time of auction is
provisional.
10. The learned Chief Standing Counsel has further placed
reliance upon the Forest Manual Volume 1 (8th Edition
2000), which according to him is presently enforced in the
State of Uttarakhand also. The Forest Manual is a
compilation of Circular and G.O. which are enforced, inter
alia, on the Sale of Goods of forest produce in U.P. as well
as in Uttarakhand. Article 152 of this Forest Manual relates
to agreement deed. Clause 8 (c) of this Article is relevant in
the present matter and the same reads as under:-

ì(8)(a)ÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖ
 (b)ÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖÖ.
 (c) The sale of lots should not be approved by
telegrams except in very exceptional
circumstances. As the ultimate responsibility for
the approval of the sale lies with the
Conservator, he should await the report of the
auctions from the D.F.O.s and should compare
the auction bids with the confidential reports in
each case and should approve the sale only after
going into the full facts of each case. The
Conservator should wait at least for a fortnight
for any complaints and representations with
regard to the auction sales and take them into
account before final approval to the sales is given
after scrutinizing the auction report from the
D.F.O.sî

7
11. Not only this, the learned Chief Standing Counsel has
taken this Court to the Act under which the actual sale of
resin is being done both in U.P. and Uttarakhand, namely,
the Uttar Pradesh Resin and other Forest Produce
(Regulation of Trade) Ordinance, 1976. The object and
reasons of the same reads as under:-
ì19.The State Government may, by notification in
the Gazette, make rules for carrying out purposes of this
Chapter.
(2) In the particular, and without prejudice to the
generality of the foregoing power, such rules may
provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:-
(a) the publication of the price list of the resin;
(b) the manner of holding inquiries under this
Chapter;
(c) the authority by whom, the manner in which
and the conditions subject to which permits may be
issued under section 5 and the fees payable for such
permits;
(d) the disposal of the resin, the purchase of which
was refused under section 8;
(e) the manner of tapping the trees for resin under
Section 9;
(f) the manner of registration under section 10, the
period within which such registration shall be made,
and the fees payable therefor;
(g) specifications of resin for purposes of
determination of quality;
(h) any other matter which is to be or may be
prescribed.
(3) All rules made under this Chapter shall as soon
as may be after they are made be laid before each
House of the State Legislature, while it is in session, for
a total period of not less than thirty days, comprised in
its one session or two or more successive sessions, and
shall, unless some later date is appointed, take effect
from the date of their publication in the Gazette, subject
to such modifications or annulments as the two Houses
of the Legislature may during the said period agree to
make, so however, that any such modification or
annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of
anything previously done thereunder.
(4) Notwithstanding anything in sub-section (3),
any rules made within one year from the
commencement of this Ordinance may be made

8
retrospectively to a date not earlier than such
commencement.î
12. The resin being forest produce is being regulated
under Section 3 of the Act. Section 3 reads as follows:-
ì3. The State Government may by notification in
the Gazette divide the State into such numbers of units,
as it may deem fit, and until varied by such notification,
each forest circle (as for the time being delimited by
general or special orders of the State Government) shall
constitute a unit.î
13. The learned Chief Standing Counsel would, hence,
argue that the unit under which the resin is sold is a
ìcircleî and all the actions including sale of resin is to be
done under the final authority of Conservator of Forest.
Therefore, the argument of the petitioner that Conservator
of Forest has absolutely no authority in the present matter
is not correct. A general reading of the provisions pointed
out by the learned C.S.C. that though for all practical
purposes Divisional Forest Officer is the competent
authority but such an authority is always subject to the
final approval of the Conservator of Forest and the
Conservator of Forest is well within its power either to
sanction or refuse to grant sanction to the sale made by the
Divisional Forest Officer. In case the Conservator of Forest
in his wisdom thinks that it is neither in the interest of
department or the State to grant such approval he must
assign reasons for doing so. In the present case these
reasons have been assigned by the Conservator of Forest.
As there is apparently much difference between the bid
given by the petitioner and which is given by other persons
in the nearby forest circles such as Champawat and
Almora, reference of which has already been given above.

and would argue that under the law presently prevalent
all sales which are made by way of auction are to be
governed by the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 and Section 64
of this Act stipulates that the sale is complete on the fall
of hammer and, therefore, all Rules, Government Orders
etc. which are contrary to the said provision have to be
discarded.
15. This argument of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is also not correct, as the entire reading of
Section 64 (2) states that an auction is complete on the
fall of hammer or in other ìcustomary mannerî and,
until such announcement is made, any bidder may
retract his bid.
16. In the present case not only the procedure and the
method which has been adopted is contained not only
in the bid condition but also in the prevalent conditions
which has been mentioned in the bid condition. The
sale which is made by the Divisional Forest Officer
would only become sale in the eyes of law when it gets

10
approval of the Conservator of Forest. Therefore,
provision of Section 64 (2) of the Act would also not help
the petitioner.
 Moreover, the order of Conservator of Forest is in
Public Interest. He has seen the difference in the
prevailing price of ìresinî and the price at which it is
being given to the petitioner, where there is a huge
difference. His action, therefore, is only in the interest of
State exchequer.
17. In the above circumstances, there is no force in
the writ petition. The writ petition fails and the same is
dismissed.
18. Learned counsel for the petitioner says that he
would be filing a Special Appeal against this order,
therefore, the effect and operation of this order shall
remain in abeyance for a period of three weeks from
today. This Court has also been informed by the learned
Chief Standing Counsel that subsequent to the auction
in question, the same resin was put for auction again
and in that auction they have received much higher
price. However, by an interim order of this Court the
respondents have been restrained from finalizing the
bid. The operation of this order is hereby kept in
abeyance for four weeks from today, which would mean
that till that period, the Forest Authorities shall not
finalize the bid.
 (Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.)
 30.10.2013
